::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 7) you can:

1. **define** GraphSAGE (sampling + aggregator variants), GAT (attention coefficients, multi-head), and GIN (sum + MLP), and compute each update by hand on toy graphs;
2. **compare** mean, max, and sum aggregators: which multisets each confuses, and which tasks that dooms;
3. **justify** each architectural component — skips, jumping knowledge, normalizations, DropEdge — by the failure mode it repairs, with the failure demonstrated rather than asserted;
4. **read** a GNN architecture description in a paper and reimplement it from the equations (including reading it critically — this lecture catches a famous one);
5. **design and run** a controlled ablation: one factor at a time, multiple seeds, error bars, and a claim that survives its own evidence.
:::

## One equation, a thousand papers

Something strange happened after 2017. The GCN paper landed, worked, and within three
years the literature filled with hundreds of "novel architectures": a convolution
here, an attention there, a pooling, a gating, an aggregation, each with its own name,
its own diagram, and its own claimed one-point victory on a benchmark whose noise
floor, as you will measure today, is about a point. A newcomer opening the
proceedings could be forgiven for despair — surely nobody can learn six hundred
architectures, and surely not all six hundred can be the state of the art.

Nobody needs to. In 2017, the *Neural Message Passing* paper
([Gilmer et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.01212)) made an observation that
deflated and organized the entire zoo at once: almost every one of those
architectures is the **same algorithm** — collect messages from neighbors, aggregate
them, update yourself — with different choices plugged into three slots. Learn the
template and the slots, and a "novel architecture" becomes a row in a table you can
read in ten seconds. This lecture is that table, its four most important rows, and —
because a design space with $10^5$ corners cannot be navigated by folklore — the
experimental discipline for choosing among them.

There is a second, quieter reason this lecture ends in methodology rather than in a
recommended architecture. When the field finally ran the fair, massive comparison
(315,000 configurations; the optional reading), the headline was not "architecture X
wins" — no architecture won. The transferable findings were about *components*
(skips help; sum aggregation travels well) and about *variance* (task-to-task
differences dwarf model-to-model ones). In a space with that shape, the durable
asset is not a favorite model but a cheap, honest procedure for deciding on *your*
task — which is a genuinely different thing to teach, and the reason this week's
lab produces a table with error bars instead of a leaderboard entry.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** Week 6's GCN treats every neighbor identically: the same
normalized weight, the same transformation, everyone averaged. Name three *distinct*
ways you might want to break that uniformity — three different senses in which
neighbors should not all count the same.

::: {.predict-answer}
The three answers are this lecture's three headline architectures. You might want to
**not read all of them** — a hub with ten thousand neighbors makes "average everyone"
a cost problem: sample instead (GraphSAGE). You might want to **weight them by
content** — some neighbors are more relevant to this node than others: learn
per-neighbor attention (GAT). And you might want to **count rather than average** —
mean throws away how *many* neighbors of each kind you have, which for some tasks is
the whole signal: sum them (GIN). Cost, relevance, multiplicity: three failures of
uniformity, three architectures.
:::
:::

Last week ended with the GCN unable to tell certain graphs apart and unable to serve
heterophilous neighborhoods — and with the promise that both wounds have treatments.
Here is the plan of treatment, which is also the plan of the lecture.

**Roadmap.** (1) The message-passing template — three slots that organize everything.
(2) GraphSAGE: sampling as a bargain, aggregators as a menu, and the inductive payoff
that finally settles Week 3's oldest debt. (3) GAT: attention on graphs, computed by
hand — and then read critically, because its most famous property is subtly broken.
(4) GIN and the aggregator question: what mean, max, and sum each forget, as theorems.
(5) The repair shop: skips, jumping knowledge, normalizations, DropEdge — each matched
to a demonstrated failure. (6) The method: ablations that produce knowledge instead of
noise, practiced on a real grid you can explore right now.

::: {.callout-note title="Recap — what this lecture assumes" collapse="true"}
- **Week 6**, thoroughly — this lecture is its direct sequel: the GCN layer
  $\hat{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}$, its low-pass reading, permutation
  equivariance, and the two failure modes at its edges (oversmoothing with depth;
  heterophily). If the renormalization trick or the $\mu^k$ decay feel hazy, reread
  Week 6 §§2–3 first; every repair in §5 leans on them.
- **Week 1**: heavy-tailed degrees (hubs are why sampling exists) and the friendship
  paradox (why sampled neighbors are not average nodes).
- **Week 2**: the WL algorithm — aggregation over *multisets* of neighbor colors; today's
  §4 is WL's question ("which multisets can you tell apart?") asked of neural
  aggregators.
- **From ML**: softmax, attention as weighted averaging (no transformer background
  needed — we build attention from scratch), batch normalization at the level of
  "normalizes activations", and recurrent nets at the level of "a sequence model
  with internal state" (LSTM/GRU — one appears as a cautionary tale in §2, one in Q1).
:::

## 1. The template: three slots

Write the general **message-passing layer** the way the MPNN paper did, and every
architecture in this lecture becomes a configuration:

$$
\mathbf{h}_v^{(k+1)} \;=\; \phi\Bigl(\mathbf{h}_v^{(k)},\;
\rho\bigl\{\psi(\mathbf{h}_u^{(k)}, \mathbf{h}_v^{(k)}, \mathbf{e}_{uv}) : u \in \mathcal{N}(v)\bigr\}\Bigr)
$$ {#eq-w07-template}

where — $\mathbf{h}_v^{(k)}$ is node $v$'s representation after $k$ layers
($\mathbf{h}_v^{(0)} = \mathbf{x}_v$, the input features); $\mathcal{N}(v)$ is $v$'s
neighbor set; $\mathbf{e}_{uv}$ is the **edge feature vector** of $(u, v)$, when the
graph carries edge features (a bond type, a relation label — absent, the argument is
simply dropped); and $\psi$, $\rho$, $\phi$ are the three learnable slots the
definition names. The braces are *multiset* braces: the aggregator sees every
message, with multiplicity, in no particular order.

::: {#def-w07-template .definition name="Message-passing template (MPNN)"}
A **message-passing layer** is any map of the form @eq-w07-template, specified by
three choices: a **message function** $\psi$ (what each neighbor sends, possibly
depending on the receiver and the edge), an **aggregator** $\rho$ (how the multiset
of messages is squashed into one vector — it must accept any number of messages in
any order, which is where Week 1's permutation demand lives), and an **update**
$\phi$ (how the node's own state meets the aggregated neighborhood). Every
architecture in this lecture is named by how it fills the three slots.
:::

Stack $K$ layers and information flows
$K$ hops, exactly as in the GCN — that part does not change all lecture.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w7-mpnn.html >}}

Three remarks before the zoo, each of which will earn its keep repeatedly. First, the
aggregator $\rho$ is the mathematically load-bearing slot: it is the only place where
the *set* nature of neighborhoods enters, so it alone decides what neighborhood
information survives — §4 makes this precise with theorems. Second, the template is a
*reading tool*: when a paper announces an architecture, find $\psi$, $\rho$, $\phi$ in
its equations and you have understood the paper's model in one pass — "specify the
three slots" is a standing exam question here precisely because it is a standing
professional skill. Third, the template is also an *implementation*: PyTorch
Geometric's `MessagePassing` base class is this equation as an API — you write
`message()`, choose an `aggr`, write `update()`, and the library handles the
scatter/gather plumbing over `edge_index`. Lab 7 has you build a layer this way from
a paper's equations, which permanently demystifies the framework.

The template also carries the field's history in miniature, which makes the
literature legible. Message passing was distilled in 2017 from four separate research
lines that had converged without noticing — spectral convolutions (Week 6's
lineage), molecular fingerprint networks in chemistry, gated recurrent graph nets,
and interaction networks in physics simulation — and the MPNN paper's contribution
was largely *taxonomy*: showing one table where the community saw many methods.
DeepMind's "graph networks" formulation
([Battaglia et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.01261)) the next year
generalized the same template to edge- and global-level states.

The software followed the taxonomy (PyTorch Geometric and DGL are both, at heart,
template engines over `edge_index`), and the architecture flood of 2018–2020 is best
read as a community sweeping the template's slots. This is the same historiographic
pattern you saw in Week 3 (every embedding a factorization) and Week 4 (every scorer
a geometry): a field's maturity moment is the arrival of the table, and after today
you hold all three tables.

One more piece of orientation: why did the field need anything beyond the GCN at all?
Three concrete pressures, each of which you have already met:

- **Scale.** Week 6's Q7 computed a full-batch GCN pass on ogbn-products; the
  arithmetic worked, but it assumed *every neighbor of every node* participates in
  every layer, and on heavy-tailed graphs (Week 1) hubs make the cost of exact
  neighborhoods both huge and wildly uneven.
- **Inductivity.** The GCN as we trained it computes on a fixed graph; Week 3's
  transductive wall (new node, no answer) was cracked but not fully broken, because
  training assumed the test graph was present.
- **Expressiveness and fit.** Week 6 §6 exhibited graphs the GCN provably cannot
  distinguish and neighborhoods (heterophilous ones) where its fixed averaging
  actively hurts.

Sampling, attention, and sum-aggregation are the respective answers, and each is one
slot's worth of change.

## 2. GraphSAGE: sample, aggregate, and finally go inductive

GraphSAGE ([Hamilton et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02216)) — from the
same Stanford group and the same year as the GCN, but aimed at industrial scale from
its first page — makes two independent moves, and it pays to hold them apart because
practitioners routinely adopt one without the other.

**Move one: a different update.** Instead of mixing self and neighborhood through one
shared transformation (the GCN's self-loop trick), SAGE keeps them separate and
concatenates:

$$
\mathbf{h}_v^{(k+1)} = \sigma\Bigl(\mathbf{W}^{(k)} \cdot
\bigl[\mathbf{h}_v^{(k)} \,\|\, \rho\{\mathbf{h}_u^{(k)} : u \in \mathcal{N}_s(v)\}\bigr]\Bigr)
$$ {#eq-w07-sage}

where — $\|$ is vector concatenation; $\mathbf{W}^{(k)}$ is the layer's weight
matrix, acting on the concatenated pair (so its left half transforms "what I am" and
its right half "what surrounds me" — equivalently, two separate matrices
$\mathbf{W}_{\text{self}}$ and $\mathbf{W}_{\text{nbr}}$ whose outputs are added);
$\rho$ is the chosen aggregator (a menu below); $\sigma$ a nonlinearity; and
$\mathcal{N}_s(v)$ is a **fixed-size sampled subset** of $\mathcal{N}(v)$ — move
two, a page from now, is entirely about that subscript $s$.

The concatenation looks like bookkeeping and is actually a design statement: the
model can now learn *different* transformations for "what I am" and "what surrounds
me" — including, in the limit, ignoring the neighborhood entirely. On a homophilous
graph that flexibility is mildly useful; on a heterophilous one it is the difference
between a model that can and cannot represent "I am the opposite of my neighbors."
File this as the first, cheapest repair for Week 6's heterophily wound (Week 10
brings stronger medicine).

Compute one update by hand, because the lab's first assert is exactly this. Take
node $C$ of the cast graph with 1-dimensional features: $h_C = 2$, neighbors
$\{A: 1, B: 3, E: 4, F: 0\}$, mean aggregator, and (scalar) weights
$\mathbf{W} = [w_{\text{self}}, w_{\text{nbr}}] = [1, \tfrac12]$, identity
activation. Aggregate: $\text{mean}(1, 3, 4, 0) = 2$. Concatenate and transform:
$1 \cdot 2 + \tfrac12 \cdot 2 = 3$. Now delete $F$ from the neighborhood and redo it:
mean becomes $8/3$, update becomes $2 + 4/3 = 10/3$ — the update moved because the
*composition* of the neighborhood moved, with the self-term untouched. Thirty seconds
of arithmetic, and you have felt the separation that the concatenation buys.

**Move two: sampled neighborhoods.** SAGE aggregates over $\mathcal{N}_s(v)$ — a
*fixed-size random sample* of neighbors (say 10 at layer one, 25 at layer two)
rather than all of them. This single change rescues minibatch training on large
graphs: with exact neighborhoods, the receptive field of one node after $K$ layers is
its full $K$-hop ball — on a small-world graph (Week 1), quickly *most of the graph*,
which is why naive minibatching explodes; with samples of size $s$, the receptive
field is at most $s^K$ nodes, a constant you chose. The price is variance: the
aggregated vector is now an *estimate* of the true neighborhood aggregate, jittering
from epoch to epoch. Feel both sides of the bargain on a real hub:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w7-sage.html >}}

The widget's spread column is doing honest statistics: the sampled mean is unbiased,
its standard deviation shrinks like $1/\sqrt{s}$, and epochs of training average over
resamples — so the noise behaves less like corruption and more like the dropout
family of regularizers, which is why in practice sampling often costs little accuracy
and occasionally *helps*. Notice also the widget's asymmetry, which is Week 1's
friendship paradox cashing in: sampling only bites on hubs, and on heavy-tailed
graphs, hubs are where all the cost was anyway.

It is worth being concrete about what a sampled *minibatch* actually is, because the
mental picture differs from every other deep-learning pipeline you know and the
difference causes real confusion in Lab 7's arxiv half. In image training, a batch
is 256 independent examples. In graph training, a batch of 256 *target nodes* is not
enough to compute anything — layer $K$ needs their sampled neighbors, layer $K{-}1$
needs the neighbors' neighbors, and so on: the batch is really a **computation
subgraph**, built backwards from the targets, containing every node any layer will
touch. Hamilton et al.'s Algorithm 1 is exactly this procedure; here it is in the
separated-weights form you will implement in Lab 7:

::: {#alg-w07-sage-minibatch .algorithm name="GraphSAGE Minibatch Forward"}
Computes $K$-layer embeddings for a batch of target nodes from sampled
neighborhoods, at a cost bounded by the fan-outs.

**Input:** target nodes $B \subseteq V$; fan-outs $s_1, \dots, s_K$; features $\mathbf{x}$; weights $\mathbf{W}^{(k)}_{\text{self}}, \mathbf{W}^{(k)}_{\text{nbr}}$ for $k = 1, \dots, K$. **Output:** embeddings $\mathbf{h}_v^{(K)}$ for all $v \in B$.

1. $B_K \leftarrow B$
2. **for** $k = K, \dots, 1$ **do** &emsp;(build the computation subgraph backwards)
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each $v \in B_k$: draw $\mathcal{N}_s(v) \subseteq \mathcal{N}(v)$ with $|\mathcal{N}_s(v)| = s_k$
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$B_{k-1} \leftarrow B_k \cup \bigcup_{v \in B_k} \mathcal{N}_s(v)$
5. **end for**
6. $\mathbf{h}_v^{(0)} \leftarrow \mathbf{x}_v$ for all $v \in B_0$
7. **for** $k = 1, \dots, K$ **do** &emsp;(now run the layers forwards)
8. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each $v \in B_k$ **do**
9. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\mathbf{m} \leftarrow \operatorname{mean}\{\mathbf{h}_u^{(k-1)} : u \in \mathcal{N}_s(v)\}$
10. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\mathbf{h}_v^{(k)} \leftarrow \sigma\bigl(\mathbf{W}^{(k)}_{\text{self}} \mathbf{h}_v^{(k-1)} + \mathbf{W}^{(k)}_{\text{nbr}}\, \mathbf{m}\bigr)$
11. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**end for**
12. **end for**
13. **return** $\{\mathbf{h}_v^{(K)} : v \in B\}$
:::

Lines 2–5 are why GNN minibatches are enormous relative to their target count: with
fan-outs $(25, 10)$ for a 2-layer model, 256 targets can pull in tens of thousands
of supporting nodes — which is fine (that was the point: the pull is *bounded* by
$\prod_k s_k$ per target, where exact neighborhoods were not bounded at all), and it
is also why shallow models are disproportionately cheap. Line 10 is @eq-w07-sage
with the concatenation multiplied out — the exact `lin_self` + `lin_nbr` pair of Lab
7's `MessagePassing` exercise, so the algorithm you just read is the code you will
write.

The backward-built subgraph also explains a serving trick worth knowing: at
inference time you can drop sampling entirely and compute exact layer-by-layer
passes over the full graph (no gradients, so memory is manageable) — train
stochastic, serve exact, and the train/serve mismatch is one more reason sampled
training's noise-tolerance matters.

**The aggregator menu.** SAGE shipped with three $\rho$ options:

- **mean** — the default, GCN-adjacent: average the sampled neighbors.
- **max-pooling** — transform each neighbor with a small MLP, take coordinatewise
  max: "is any neighbor strongly X?"
- **LSTM** — run the neighbors through a sequence model.

The LSTM aggregator deserves a moment of
critical reading practice, three sections before we do it to GAT: an LSTM consumes a
*sequence*, but a neighborhood is a *set* — so SAGE feeds neighbors in random order
and hopes the LSTM learns approximate order-invariance. It scored well on benchmarks;
it also violates the one structural commitment (permutation invariance, Week 1) that
every other component of every architecture in this course respects by construction.
The field quietly dropped it. The lesson is not "LSTMs are bad" — it is that
benchmark wins do not certify structural correctness, and you now know to check the
$\rho$ slot of any new paper for exactly this sin.

A budgeting aside that interviews love and papers omit: compare parameter counts
across the regimes this course has visited. Week 3's lookup table: $O(nd)$ — half a
terabyte at social scale. A SAGE layer: two weight matrices, $O(d \cdot d')$ —
*independent of the graph entirely*; a full model is a few hundred thousand
parameters whether the graph has thirty-four nodes or three billion. That inversion
— parameters scale with feature width, data scales with the graph — is why GNNs are
statistically thrifty on large graphs (many nodes supervising few weights) and
prone to overfitting on tiny ones (Cora's 140 training labels supervising those
same weights, which is why dropout and small hidden sizes dominate its
leaderboard). One architecture family, two opposite failure regimes, both predicted
by counting.

**The inductive payoff.** Here is the sentence Week 3 has been waiting four weeks
for, promoted at last to the formal status it earns today:

::: {#def-w07-inductive .definition name="Inductive vs. transductive model"}
A graph model is **transductive** if its predictions are defined only for the nodes
present at training time — Week 3's lookup tables, where the embedding *is* the
parameter. It is **inductive** if it defines a function that can be evaluated on any
graph over the same feature space: new nodes, new edges, an entirely new graph —
embed them by running the forward pass. The test to apply: ask where the parameters
live. Per-node parameters ⇒ transductive; parameters only in shared functions ⇒
inductive.
:::

Because every SAGE parameter lives in the *functions* ($\mathbf{W}$s and
aggregators) and none in a per-node table, a trained SAGE model is a program you can
run on **any graph with the same feature space**. The original paper's flagship
experiment trained on one protein–protein interaction graph and predicted on
*different organisms' graphs*; the modern deployment pattern — train weekly, serve
continuously on a growing graph — is only possible in this regime. Week 3's wall #2
is now rubble: the encoder computes instead of remembering. (Walls #1, #3, and #4
fell with it: parameters shared, features consumed, size $O(1)$ in $n$ — the entire
critique of the lookup table, answered by one architectural decision.)

## 3. GAT: attention, derived and then interrogated

If neighbors should not count equally, let the model decide how much each counts.
GAT ([Veličković et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10903)) — arriving the
year attention was eating natural language processing, and importing the idea with
graph-shaped adjustments — changes exactly one slot:

::: {#def-w07-gat .definition name="GAT attention layer"}
A **GAT layer** computes, for each edge $(u, v)$, an **attention coefficient**, then
aggregates neighbors with those learned weights:

$$
e_{vu} = \text{LeakyReLU}\bigl(\mathbf{a}^\top [\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_v \,\|\, \mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_u]\bigr),
\qquad
\alpha_{vu} = \frac{\exp(e_{vu})}{\sum_{u' \in \mathcal{N}(v) \cup \{v\}} \exp(e_{vu'})},
\qquad
\mathbf{h}_v' = \sigma\Bigl(\sum_{u} \alpha_{vu}\, \mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_u\Bigr).
$$ {#eq-w07-gat}

Read it as three moves: score every edge ($e$), let the scores compete ($\alpha$ —
a softmax over the neighborhood, self included), average with the winners'
weights ($\mathbf{h}'$).
:::

where — $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d' \times d}$ is the shared linear map applied
to every node; $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^{2d'}$ is the learned **attention vector**
that scores a (receiver, sender) pair; $\|$ is concatenation; LeakyReLU is
$\max(x, 0.2x)$ (leaky so that negative scores keep a gradient); and the softmax
runs over $\mathcal{N}(v) \cup \{v\}$, so the node attends to itself alongside its
neighbors. In template terms: $\psi$ is the shared linear map, $\rho$
is a *learned-weighted* mean, $\phi$ is the nonlinearity — one slot changed, and the
change is that aggregation weights now depend on *content*, not just on degree
bookkeeping as the GCN's $1/\sqrt{\hat d_u \hat d_v}$ did.

Hand-compute one attention head, because the mechanics compress three papers into one
example. Let $v$ have two neighbors with (already transformed, 2-dim) features
$\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_{u_1} = (1, 0)$, $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_{u_2} = (0, 1)$, self
$\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_v = (1, 1)$, and attention vector
$\mathbf{a} = (1, 0, 2, 0)$ — i.e., $\mathbf{a}$ reads the first coordinate of the
receiver and the first coordinate of the sender, weighting the sender double. Scores:
$e_{vv} = \text{LReLU}(1 + 2 \cdot 1) = 3$; $e_{vu_1} = \text{LReLU}(1 + 2 \cdot 1) = 3$;
$e_{vu_2} = \text{LReLU}(1 + 2 \cdot 0) = 1$. Softmax over $\{3, 3, 1\}$:
$\alpha \approx (0.47, 0.47, 0.06)$ — the second neighbor, whose content lacks what
$\mathbf{a}$ looks for, is nearly muted. That muting is the sales pitch: on a
heterophilous fringe, an attention head can learn to down-weight misleading
neighbors, something no fixed normalization can do. **Multi-head** attention runs $H$
independent $(\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{a})$ pairs and concatenates the results — the same
role channels play in a CNN: different heads free to specialize in different
neighbor-selection criteria, plus a variance-reduction effect that makes training
tangibly more stable.

Now the critical reading, because GAT is this course's designated case study in
*reading a famous architecture skeptically*. Look at the score formula in
@eq-w07-gat again and split the pre-activation:

$$
e_{vu} = \text{LReLU}\bigl(\underbrace{\mathbf{a}_1^\top \mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_v}_{\text{receiver term}} + \underbrace{\mathbf{a}_2^\top \mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_u}_{\text{sender term}}\bigr)
$$ {#eq-w07-split}

where — $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d'}$ are simply the first and
second halves of the attention vector $\mathbf{a}$, and LReLU abbreviates LeakyReLU.
Nothing new was introduced: the concatenation in @eq-w07-gat *is* this sum. But the
split exposes everything —

::: {#prp-static .proposition name="GAT's attention is static"}
For a fixed receiver $v$, the ranking of senders $u$ by $e_{vu}$ is determined by the
sender term $\mathbf{a}_2^\top \mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_u$ alone — the *same* ranking for
every receiver. Consequently GAT cannot represent any attention pattern in which
different receivers prefer different senders (e.g., "query $i$ attends to key $i$").
:::

<details><summary>Proof (monotonicity does all the work)</summary>
Fix $v$; the receiver term is a constant $c_v$ across senders, so
$e_{vu} = \text{LReLU}(c_v + s_u)$ with $s_u = \mathbf{a}_2^\top \mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_u$.
LeakyReLU is strictly increasing, and adding a constant preserves order, so
$e_{vu} > e_{vu'} \iff s_u > s_{u'}$ — an ordering independent of $v$. Softmax is
also order-preserving, so every receiver's attention distribution peaks on the same
globally-best sender. A "dictionary lookup" pattern (receiver $i$ peaks on sender
$i$) requires $n$ different orderings; GAT has one. $\square$
</details>

The repair — GATv2 ([Brody et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14491)) — is a
single line: apply the nonlinearity *before* the attention vector,

$$
e_{vu} = \mathbf{a}^\top\, \text{LReLU}\bigl(\mathbf{W} [\mathbf{h}_v \,\|\, \mathbf{h}_u]\bigr)
$$ {#eq-w07-gatv2}

where — $\mathbf{W}$ now multiplies the *concatenated* pair (mixing receiver and
sender before the nonlinearity acts) and $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^{d'}$ scores the
mixed vector. Receiver and sender interact inside the nonlinearity, the score no
longer splits as @eq-w07-split, and the separation argument dies. Watch the
proposition and its repair happen — both models trained live, same task, same seed:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w7-gat.html >}}

Three durable morals from one widget. Practically: use GATv2 — it is the same cost
and strictly more expressive; PyG ships both. Empirically: GAT *still helped* on many
real benchmarks for years, because homophilous node classification rarely needs
per-receiver rankings — a flaw can be real and rarely triggered, which is why
benchmarks alone never found it. Methodologically: the flaw was found by *reading the
equations* and constructing the minimal failing task — the exact skill objective 4
names, demonstrated at the level where it earned a publication.

Four working notes complete the attention picture, each one line of code in the lab
and one sentence of judgment here.

1. **Cost.** Attention computes one score per edge per head — $O(mHd)$, with $m$
   the number of edges and $H$ the number of heads — so it scales exactly as well as
   sparsity allows and exactly as badly as hubs demand; combined with sampling it
   inherits SAGE's bargain unchanged.
2. **Edge features.** The score has an obvious third input slot —
   $e_{vu} = f(\mathbf{h}_v, \mathbf{h}_u, \mathbf{e}_{vu})$ — and attention is the
   most natural place in the whole template to inject edge attributes (bond types in
   Week 13's molecules, relation types in Week 10's heterogeneous graphs both enter
   here).
3. **Attention dropout.** Randomly zeroing attention coefficients during training is
   GAT's own regularizer, and it composes with (rather than replaces) DropEdge — one
   drops *scores*, the other drops *structure*.
4. **When to expect a win.** Attention earns its parameters where neighbor
   *relevance genuinely varies* — heterophilous fringes, noisy edges from LLM
   extraction (Week 5's precision failures arriving as graph input!),
   multi-relational data — and tends to tie with mean aggregation where homophily is
   strong and edges are curated, which the measured grid in §6 will confirm on Cora
   with error bars.

## 4. GIN and the aggregator question

Strip away sampling and attention and one question remains at the bottom of the
design space, and it is Week 2's question wearing feature vectors: **which multisets
of neighbors can your aggregator tell apart?** WL answered it for colors with a
perfect (injective) hash. Neural aggregators are not perfect hashes, and their
imperfections are exactly characterizable:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w7-aggregators.html >}}

::: {#prp-agg .proposition name="What mean, max, and sum forget"}
Over multisets of one-hot features: **mean** determines exactly the *proportions* of
each type (it confuses any two multisets that are scalings of each other, e.g.
$\{t\}$ vs $\{t, t\}$); **max** determines exactly the *support* — which types are
present at all (it confuses any two multisets with equal support, regardless of
counts); **sum** determines the multiset exactly (counts of every type), and is the
only one of the three that does.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (each claim in one line)</summary>
With one-hot features, coordinate $i$ of the sum is the count $c_i$ of type $i$ — the
multiset itself. Coordinate $i$ of the mean is $c_i / \sum_j c_j$ — the proportion
vector, unchanged by scaling all counts; conversely equal proportions with different
totals give equal means, so mean determines exactly proportions. Coordinate $i$ of
the max is $\mathbb{1}[c_i > 0]$ — the support indicator, and nothing more. $\square$
</details>

Play the game yourself — and try the widget's standing challenge, which quietly
previews a Week 9 subtlety:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w7-agg.html >}}

**GIN** ([Xu et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00826)) — the Graph
Isomorphism Network, and the name is a thesis statement:
this is the architecture designed backwards from the question "what would it take to
match WL?" rather than forwards from a benchmark. It takes the proposition seriously
in all three slots:

::: {#def-w07-gin .definition name="GIN layer"}
$$
\mathbf{h}_v^{(k+1)} = \text{MLP}^{(k)}\Bigl((1 + \varepsilon^{(k)})\,\mathbf{h}_v^{(k)} + \sum_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)} \mathbf{h}_u^{(k)}\Bigr)
$$ {#eq-w07-gin}

where — $\text{MLP}^{(k)}$ is a multi-layer perceptron (at least one hidden layer)
and $\varepsilon^{(k)}$ a learnable scalar. Each design choice answers the
proposition: **sum** aggregation (keep the multiset), the $\varepsilon$-scaled
self-term (keep "me" distinguishable from "one more neighbor like me"), and an
**MLP** — not a single linear layer — as the update, because injective set
functions composed with weak function approximators stop being injective.
:::

One honest asterisk on the proposition, which is also the answer key to the
widget's standing challenge. The clean statements hold for *one-hot* (more
generally, countable) features; with arbitrary real-valued features, scalar sums can
collide ($\{1, 3\}$ and $\{2, 2\}$ sum identically — if you found that in the widget,
you found the asterisk), and injectivity must be *manufactured*: first embed each
element through a learned function, then sum — which is precisely why GIN's update
wraps the sum in an MLP, and why the underlying DeepSets result
([Zaheer et al., 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06114)) says every
well-behaved permutation-invariant set function has exactly this
embed-sum-transform shape. The engineering reading: sum is not magic, *sum after a
learned embedding* is — and the MLP is not decoration but the load-bearing half of
the injectivity argument. Week 9 turns this asterisk into the week's central
theorem.

Week 9 proves the
headline theorem — GIN is exactly as powerful as the WL test, and nothing
message-passing can do better — but the practical guidance lands today: **for
graph-level tasks where counting substructure matters (molecules above all), sum
aggregation is the consistently right default; for node classification on rich,
noisy, real-valued features, mean's normalization is often the better inductive
bias** (sums grow with degree, and degree, as always, becomes a confound —
witness what depth-4 GIN does in §6's measured grid). The aggregator is a modeling
decision about *what information the task needs preserved*, and you can now make it
by argument rather than by grid search.

## 5. The repair shop: components matched to failure modes

The second half of any modern GNN paper's architecture section is a parade of
add-ons: residual connections, jumping knowledge, three kinds of normalization,
DropEdge. Presented as a list, they read as superstition. Presented as
*failure-mode → repair* pairs, they read as engineering — so here is each failure,
demonstrated, with its repair.

**Failure: depth destroys signal.** Week 6 proved the GCN is a low-pass filter and
showed components decaying as $\mu^k$; here is what that does to representations,
measured rather than asserted — the same experiment you can rerun from the figure's
generator:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w7-oversmoothing.html >}}

By twelve propagations, plain averaging has made the karate club's members nearly
indistinguishable — mean pairwise cosine 0.96 — which is
<span class="term" data-def="Oversmoothing: the tendency of deep message-passing networks to drive all node representations toward a common value, as repeated neighborhood averaging converges to the dominant (constant-ish) eigenvector. The reason naive deep GNNs underperform shallow ones.">**oversmoothing**</span>
in one number. The repairs in the figure are the repairs in the literature.

**Residual connections** mix each layer's output with its input:

$$
\mathbf{h}^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{h}^{(k)} + f\bigl(\mathbf{h}^{(k)}\bigr)
$$ {#eq-w07-residual}

where — $f$ is the whole message-passing layer (message, aggregate, update) and the
addition is elementwise, so each layer now learns a *correction* to its input rather
than a replacement. Spectrally, residuals shift every eigenvalue
toward 1, slowing the decay; in optimization terms they give gradients a highway
past the smoothing operators. The figure shows them *delaying* collapse rather than
preventing it — an honest account you will confirm with accuracy numbers in §6.

**Restart (initial-residual) connections** — the design inside APPNP
([Gasteiger et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.05997)) and GCNII
([Chen et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.02133)) — go further, mixing a
fixed fraction of the *layer-zero* features into every layer:

$$
\mathbf{h}^{(k+1)} = \alpha\, \mathbf{h}^{(0)} + (1 - \alpha)\, \hat{\mathbf{A}}\, \mathbf{h}^{(k)}
$$ {#eq-w07-restart}

where — $\mathbf{h}^{(0)}$ is the layer-zero representation (the input features,
possibly once-transformed), $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ is the restart fraction (0.1 in the
figure), and $\hat{\mathbf{A}}$ is Week 6's normalized propagation operator. The
figure's green curve plateaus, because a fixed dose of the original signal
re-enters at every depth. If that trick smells familiar, it should: @eq-w07-restart
is PageRank's teleport, resurrected as an architecture (the same $\alpha$, the same
fixed point, Week 2 paying dividends again).

**Jumping knowledge** ([Xu et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.03536)) attacks
the problem from the side: run all $K$ layers, keep every layer's representation, and
let the final readout combine them (concat, max, or attention over depths) — so
each node effectively *chooses its own depth*, hub nodes reading shallow and
peripheral nodes reading deep.

**Failure: activations drift and explode.** Deep stacks of aggregations shift
activation statistics — GIN's sums grow with degree; attention stacks saturate — and
the generic deep-learning medicine applies: **BatchNorm** (normalize each feature
across the batch; the design-space study's most consistently helpful normalization),
**LayerNorm** (normalize within each node's vector; indifferent to batch composition,
standard in attention stacks). One norm is graph-specific and worth knowing by name:
**PairNorm** ([Zhao & Akoglu, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.12223)) keeps the
*pairwise distance* between node representations at a constant
level across layers — it is an anti-oversmoothing device by construction, useful
when you must go deep without restart tricks.

A graph-specific subtlety hides inside
the generic medicine too: with sampled minibatches, BatchNorm's "batch" is a
computation subgraph whose composition changes every step — its statistics are
noisier than in image training and biased toward whatever neighborhood mix the
sampler drew, which is one practical reason LayerNorm (batch-independent by
construction) gains ground as graphs get larger and sampling gets more aggressive.
The measured grid you are about to meet held normalization fixed precisely to keep
its factor count honest — extending it with a ±BatchNorm axis is Lab 7's designated
stretch, and the design-space study's verdict gives you the prior to bet against.

**Failure: memorizing edges.** Small graphs, big models: the network learns *this
adjacency* rather than a function of neighborhoods. **DropEdge**
([Rong et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10903)) removes a random
fraction of edges each epoch — data augmentation on structure. It also, incidentally,
thins the propagation operator (fewer edges per layer means slower mixing), so it
doubles as a mild oversmoothing brake — one mechanism, two effects, and the reason
it appears in both the regularization and the depth sections of papers. Note what it
is *not*: feature dropout — the two compose, and ablating them separately is a Lab 7
stretch goal.

The design space, assembled — with the verdicts of the field's one systematic sweep
([You, Ying & Leskovec, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.08843) — the
315,000-configuration study, this week's optional reading) attached:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w7-design.html >}}

Read the verdict column with calibrated trust: "consistently helpful" in that study
means *across many tasks under fair tuning* — it is the best prior you can buy, not a
guarantee for your graph. Which is precisely why the last section exists.

## 6. The method: ablations that produce knowledge

Every claim in §5 has the same epistemic shape: "component X helps because of
mechanism Y." The design space is too large for folklore, papers' own comparisons
are chronically confounded (new architecture + new tricks + more tuning budget,
reported as one number), and your graph is not their graph. The only trustworthy
instrument is the **controlled ablation** — and it is a *method*, with rules:

1. **One factor at a time.** Change the aggregator *or* the depth *or* the
   normalization; never two. A 2×2×2 grid of single changes beats eight bespoke
   "improved models" because every comparison in it is interpretable.
2. **Multiple seeds, always.** GNN training on small graphs is noisy — the measured
   grid below contains a configuration with a sample s.d. of 19.5 accuracy points
   across seeds ("s.d." here and throughout §6, to keep $\sigma$ for activation
   functions). A single-seed comparison on Cora is astrology.
3. **Error bars decide.** A delta smaller than roughly two standard deviations is
   "within noise", and saying so out loud is a professional skill, not a
   disappointment.
4. **Fixed budget, fixed protocol.** Same tuning effort per configuration, same
   splits, same early-stopping rule — or you are measuring your own enthusiasm.
5. **Claims cite cells.** Every sentence of your conclusion should trace to specific
   numbers in the table. "Residuals matter at depth" is legal only if the table
   contains depth-with and depth-without columns.

The five rules compress into a procedure — the course's protocol, and the one every
number in the rest of this lecture was produced by. Lab 7 hands it to you as code:
its `run()` executes lines 3–4, its `summarize()` is line 6.

::: {#alg-w07-ablation .algorithm name="One-Factor Ablation with Seeds and Error Bars"}
Produces a table of mean ± s.d. scores over a factor grid, and claims that cite it.

**Input:** factor grid $F = F_1 \times \cdots \times F_j$; seed set $S$; a fixed budget (splits, epochs, early-stop rule, tuning effort). **Output:** table $c \mapsto (\text{mean} \pm \text{s.d.})$ test accuracy; claims citing cells.

1. **for** each configuration $c \in F$ **do**
2. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each seed $s \in S$ **do**
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;initialize model($c$) with seed $s$; train under the fixed budget
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;record test accuracy at the best-*validation* epoch
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**end for**
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;table[$c$] $\leftarrow$ (mean, sample s.d.) over the seeds $S$
7. **end for**
8. **for** each claim: state the sentence, the cells, the scope
9. declare any delta below $2 \times$ s.d. "within noise"
10. **return** the table and the claims
:::

Note what the procedure refuses to permit: no configuration gets extra tuning (line
3's *fixed* budget is rule 4 as an instruction, not an aspiration), no run reports
its last epoch (line 4 evaluates where validation peaked — anything else measures
patience, not accuracy), and no comparison escapes its error bars (line 9). The cost
is the grid size times seeds; the return is that every sentence you write afterwards
traces to a cell.

Here is a real grid — sixteen configurations, three seeds each, measured with
exactly this protocol — and it teaches more than any architecture section:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w7-ablation.html >}}

Spend real minutes in this widget; it is the lecture's argument in numbers, and —
worth saying plainly — every value in it came from actual training runs under the
stated protocol, because a lecture that preaches error bars owes you its own. The
grid took about eight minutes of laptop compute, which is itself a finding: the
price of knowing instead of believing, for a question this size, is one coffee. The
findings you should extract, stated as an ablation report's conclusions:

1. **The boring baseline wins.** The 2-layer GCN is the single best cell
   (81.0 ± 0.6) — on this dataset, with this budget, no fancy architecture beats
   boring, which is Cora's famous lesson and the reason serious papers moved to
   harder benchmarks.
2. **At depth 4, residuals are a resurrection, not an optimization.** GAT goes from
   26.2 ± 9.8 (a crash, with seed-to-seed chaos) to 80.5 ± 1.0 — a **+54-point**
   swing from one skip connection — while GIN's 44.2 ± 19.5 is a model gambling.
3. **At depth 2, residuals change nothing anywhere** (every delta within noise) —
   the repair is real *and* conditional, which is exactly what §5's mechanism story
   predicts: there is no depth to rescue.
4. **Celebrated architecture differences sit under the noise floor.** GCN vs SAGE
   at depth 2: 81.0 vs 79.8, overlapping error bars — and sentence-length claims in
   papers routinely rest on smaller gaps.

And the meta-lesson
over all four: *none of these findings could be stated from a single run of a single
model*, which is the entire case for the method.

And because an ablation is only as good as its write-up, the reporting template —
which Lab 7 grades against, and which serves unchanged in industry design docs and
paper rebuttals alike. A claims paragraph has three moves per claim:

- **The sentence.** "Residual connections are necessary at depth 4."
- **The cells.** "GAT: 26.2 ± 9.8 → 80.5 ± 1.0; GIN: 44.2 ± 19.5 → 75.2 ± 1.3."
- **The scope.** "Cora, this protocol; untested beyond depth 4."

Three disciplines around it: report every cell
you ran (a table with holes invites the suspicion it deserves); state the protocol
once, completely (splits, budget, stopping rule, seeds) so the grid is reproducible
from the paragraph; and write the negative findings with the same care ("SAGE vs GCN:
indistinguishable at depth 2") — negative cells are the cheapest leak-proof knowledge
your compute budget produces, and senior reviewers read them first.

A note on scale, because the lab pairs Cora with ogbn-arxiv (170k nodes — Cora ×60)
and the design conclusions shift with size: bigger graphs support deeper models
before oversmoothing bites (more diverse neighborhoods to average), sampling stops
being optional (full-batch fits neither memory nor patience), the noise floor drops
(bigger test sets, tighter error bars — real architecture differences become
resolvable), and boring baselines stop winning automatically. "What changes when the
graph is 100× bigger" is this week's lab question, and Week 11 makes scale the whole
topic.

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 1 · Architecture shopping" icon="false"}
Reading leaderboards as menus — "GAT beat GCN on Cora, so we use GAT" — imports
conclusions across graphs, tasks, and tuning budgets that do not transfer (the
measured grid above has GAT *below* GCN in every matched cell). The professional
move: pick the simplest architecture whose *mechanisms* match your task's needs
(§2–§4 gave you the mechanism-to-need map), then ablate on *your* data.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 2 · Depth as a virtue" icon="false"}
CNN intuition says deeper is better; message passing says deeper is *smoother* —
receptive fields explode on small-world graphs (Week 1) and representations collapse
(the measured curves). Most published GNNs are 2–4 layers deep for a reason. Go
deeper only with a mechanism that pays for it (restart connections, PairNorm, JK) and
an ablation showing depth actually bought accuracy on your task.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 3 · The unread ρ slot" icon="false"}
Aggregators get chosen by library default, yet they set the information ceiling
(@prp-agg): mean silently deletes counts your molecular task needs; sum silently
imports a degree confound your social task will exploit as leakage. When results
disappoint, read the ρ slot before adding parameters — the failure is often
representational, not statistical, and no amount of training fixes "the information
was deleted in layer one."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 4 · Trusting attention weights as explanations" icon="false"}
Attention coefficients are seductive: they look like "the model showing its
reasoning". They are learned weights entangled with everything else — @prp-static
showed a whole architecture whose weights *could not* express the preferences people
read into them, and even dynamic attention redistributes freely among correlated
neighbors. Treat α's as diagnostics to investigate, never as explanations to ship;
if stakeholders need explanations, that is a separate requirement with separate
tooling.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 5 · The ablation you didn't run" icon="false"}
The mirror image of Pitfall 1: shipping your *own* improvement on a single seed and
a favorable configuration. The grid above contains a ready-made cautionary tale —
at one seed, depth-4 GIN can land anywhere in a 40-point range. If your improvement
paper would not survive rule 2 and rule 3 of §6, it is not yet a result; it is an
anecdote with a confidence interval you declined to compute.
:::

and an `aggr` argument; the aggregator-confusion demonstration run as code; and then

## Required reading

**1 · Hamilton, Ying & Leskovec — *Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs* (NeurIPS 2017).** [arXiv:1706.02216](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.02216)

::: {.reading-annotation}
GraphSAGE. Work through Algorithm 1 line by line — it is §2's two moves in
pseudocode — and be able to say why fixed-size sampling bounds the minibatch cost
(the $s^K$ argument). Compare the aggregator variants in §3.3 against today's
@prp-agg, and read the LSTM aggregator with your critical-reading hat on: what
property does it violate? The inductive experiments (Reddit, cross-organism PPI) are
the payoff — skim the clustering-coefficient theory in §3.4.
:::

**2 · Veličković et al. — *Graph Attention Networks* (ICLR 2018).** [arXiv:1710.10903](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10903)

::: {.reading-annotation}
GAT. Derive the attention coefficients from §2.1 and Figure 1 by hand until the
lecture's worked example feels routine; note how multi-head attention plays the role
channels play in CNNs, and how self-attention includes the node itself. Then — after
today — reread §2.1 knowing @prp-static, and find the exact equation where the
static-attention limitation hides. Reading a landmark paper twice, once naively and
once armed, is the week's real assignment.
:::

**Also see:** Hamilton, *GRL book*, ch. 5 (the neighborhood-aggregation design
space; our slot notation follows it) · CS224W, "A General Perspective on GNNs".

**Optional:** Xu et al., [How Powerful are GNNs?](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.00826)
(ICLR 2019) — this week, read only Figures 2–3 and §4.1 for the aggregator
intuition; Week 9 does the theorems · You, Ying & Leskovec,
[Design Space for GNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.08843) (NeurIPS 2020) — the
315,000-configuration study behind Figure 4's verdicts; read §3 and the ranking
analysis · Brody, Alon & Yahav,
[How Attentive are GATs?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14491) (ICLR 2022) — the
static-attention critique and the one-line fix; §3 is today's @prp-static at full
strength · Rong et al., [DropEdge](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10903) (ICLR 2020) —
the regularization corner; read §§1, 3.1, 4.1–4.2 and take the over-smoothing
theorems on faith.

## Check your understanding

<details><summary>Q1 · The template — A paper defines its layer as: "each edge computes a gate g = σ(wᵀ[hᵤ ‖ hᵥ]); node v sums g·hᵤ over neighbors and passes the result through a GRU with its previous state." Identify ψ, ρ, φ, and name the closest architecture from this lecture.</summary>
$\psi(h_u, h_v) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top[h_u \| h_v]) \cdot h_u$ — a
receiver-conditioned gated message; $\rho$ = sum; $\phi$ = GRU(previous state,
aggregate). Closest relative: GAT — a content-dependent per-edge weight times the
neighbor — but with a sigmoid *gate* instead of a softmax (weights need not compete
or sum to 1: an "absolute relevance" rather than "relative attention" design), plus
a recurrent update. If you can produce this paragraph for an arbitrary paper, the
zoo is yours; this is objective 4's exam form.
</details>

<details><summary>Q2 · Hand computation — Node v: h_v = (1, 1); neighbors (2, 0) and (0, 2). Compute h′_v under (a) SAGE-mean with W = I on both halves (i.e., self + mean), identity activation; (b) GIN with ε = 0 and identity MLP; (c) GAT with uniform attention over {v, u₁, u₂} and W = I. Then explain which pair of answers must coincide and why.</summary>
Mean of neighbors: $(1, 1)$. (a) $\text{self} + \text{mean} = (1,1) + (1,1) = (2, 2)$.
(b) $\text{self} + \text{sum} = (1,1) + (2,2) = (3, 3)$. (c) uniform attention over
three vectors including self: $\tfrac13[(1,1) + (2,0) + (0,2)] = (1, 1)$. None
coincide here — but (a) and (c) *would* coincide if GAT's softmax happened to put
weight ½ on self and ¼ on each neighbor: attention with content-blind weights
degenerates to a normalized mean, which is the formal sense in which GAT generalizes
GCN/SAGE-mean and GIN does not (sum is not a weighted mean — its output scale grows
with degree, as (b)'s larger numbers show).
</details>

<details><summary>Q3 · Aggregator selection — For each task, choose mean, max, or sum, and defend with @prp-agg: (a) "is this molecule aromatic?" (needs ring-atom counts); (b) "is this account in contact with ANY sanctioned entity?"; (c) "classify a paper's field given neighbors with rich text embeddings"; (d) "predict a protein's degree-correlated abundance."</summary>
(a) **Sum** — counts are the signal; mean would report ring *proportions* and max
mere presence. (b) **Max** — the task IS the support question; sum/mean would let
many innocuous neighbors dilute one crucial contact. (c) **Mean** — with real-valued
embeddings, proportions/centroids of the neighborhood are the robust signal and
degree normalization removes a confound. (d) Trick entry: sum *encodes* degree, so it
"helps" — but ask whether you want the model to learn abundance-from-degree (a
shortcut that breaks under distribution shift) or provide degree as an explicit
feature and keep mean. Aggregator choice is modeling, not tuning.
</details>

<details><summary>Q4 · Prove-it — Show that GAT with a single head cannot solve the dictionary task for n ≥ 3 (query i must put its argmax on key i), no matter the training. Then explain in one sentence why GATv2's reordering breaks your proof.</summary>
By @prp-static's argument: for fixed receiver, sender ranking is induced by
$s_u = \mathbf{a}_2^\top \mathbf{W} \mathbf{h}_u$, which is receiver-independent;
so all queries share one argmax sender (ties aside), and at most one query can be
correct — $1 < n$. GATv2 computes
$\mathbf{a}^\top \text{LReLU}(\mathbf{W}[\mathbf{h}_v \| \mathbf{h}_u])$: the
nonlinearity acts on a *joint* function of receiver and sender, so the score no
longer splits into (receiver constant) + (sender term), and no receiver-independent
ranking is forced. The widget is this proof running with gradient descent as the
adversary.
</details>

<details><summary>Q5 · Mechanism matching — A 6-layer GCN on a citation graph trains to 30% accuracy (2-layer: 78%). For each observation, name the diagnosis and the first repair you would ablate: (a) all node representations have pairwise cosine > 0.95 at layer 6; (b) training loss oscillates wildly between epochs; (c) the model fits train perfectly but transfers terribly to next year's papers.</summary>
(a) Oversmoothing (the measured curves' regime) → residual or restart connections
(or JK); PairNorm as alternative. (b) Optimization instability — deep unnormalized
stacks → BatchNorm/LayerNorm first, learning-rate second. (c) Structure memorization
/ distribution shift → DropEdge + evaluate with a temporal split (the Week 1
discipline; "next year's papers" is a time split whether you honor it or not). The
skill being tested: components are indexed by failure modes, not by fashion.
</details>

<details><summary>Q6 · Read the grid — Using Figure 4's measured numbers: (a) is "SAGE beats GCN on Cora" defensible at depth 2? (b) What is the single largest effect in the entire grid, and what claim does it license? (c) A blog post says "GIN is unstable." What is the honest, cell-cited version of that sentence?</summary>
(a) No: 79.8 ± 1.1 vs 81.0 ± 0.6 — GCN is nominally *ahead*, and the gap is within
joint noise; the defensible sentence is "indistinguishable under this protocol".
(b) GAT at depth 4: 26.2 ± 9.8 without residuals vs 80.5 ± 1.0 with — a +54.3
swing; it licenses "at depth 4 on Cora, residual connections determine whether GAT
trains at all", and nothing broader. (c) "Depth-4 GIN without skips shows extreme
seed variance on Cora (44.2 ± 19.5); at depth 2, or with residuals, its variance is
ordinary (≈ ±1)." Precision about *which cell* is the entire difference between
knowledge and vibes.
</details>

<details><summary>Q7 · Inductive stakes — Your team trained a SAGE model on January's transaction graph. In March, the graph has 20% new accounts and a new merchant category. List what the model can do without retraining, what silently degrades, and what breaks — and contrast each line with the Week 3 lookup-table world.</summary>
Can do: embed and score every new account/edge by running the forward pass — the
lookup table could not emit anything for them. Degrades silently: distribution shift
— the new merchant category produces feature patterns unseen in training, so the
*function* runs but its outputs drift from calibration (monitor with a fixed probe
population, Week 3's production discipline transfers). Breaks: any change to the
*feature schema* (new feature dimensions) — inductivity is over graphs, not over
input spaces; and shifts in the label relationship itself require retraining in both
worlds. The honest summary: SAGE converts "cannot answer" into "answers with aging
confidence" — a huge upgrade that must still be operated, not trusted.
</details>

<details><summary>Q8 · Design a study — You have one week and a GPU to decide an architecture for molecular toxicity (graph-level, 40k molecules). Specify your ablation: factors and levels, what stays fixed, seeds, the metric, and the two mistakes from this lecture you are most at risk of making.</summary>
One defensible design: factors = aggregator {mean, sum} × depth {3, 5} ×
{±BatchNorm}, with architecture fixed to GIN-style layers (the mechanism argument —
counting substructure — already picks the family, so spend the budget inside it);
fixed: hidden size, optimizer, budgeted early stopping, scaffold split (chemistry's
honest split — random splits leak series of similar molecules); 3–5 seeds; metric
ROC-AUC with mean ± std. Risks: Pitfall 3 in reverse — sum's degree signal may
shortcut on molecule size, so add a size-stratified analysis; and rule 4 violations
— it is fatally tempting to give your favorite cell one extra tuning pass. A
one-week study run this way beats a month of architecture shopping, which is the
lecture's closing claim in operational form.
</details>

::: {.notions}
**Notions introduced this week**

- **Message-passing template** (@def-w07-template, @eq-w07-template) — message $\psi$ / aggregate $\rho$ / update $\phi$; every architecture is a way of filling the slots.
- **GraphSAGE layer** (@eq-w07-sage) — separate self/neighbor transforms, concatenated; sampled neighborhoods $\mathcal{N}_s(v)$.
- **Computation subgraph / minibatch forward** (@alg-w07-sage-minibatch) — the batch built backwards from the targets; cost bounded by the fan-outs.
- **Inductive vs. transductive** (@def-w07-inductive) — parameters in shared functions vs. per-node tables; Week 3's wall, formally demolished.
- **GAT attention** (@def-w07-gat, @eq-w07-gat) — learned, content-dependent neighbor weights; multi-head = channels.
- **Static attention** (@prp-static, @eq-w07-split) — GAT's score splits into receiver + sender terms, forcing one sender ranking for all receivers; GATv2 (@eq-w07-gatv2) reorders one line to fix it.
- **Aggregator expressiveness** (@prp-agg) — sum keeps counts, mean keeps proportions, max keeps presence.
- **GIN layer** (@def-w07-gin, @eq-w07-gin) — sum + $\varepsilon$-scaled self-term + MLP: the WL-matching design.
- **Oversmoothing repairs** (@eq-w07-residual, @eq-w07-restart) — residuals delay collapse; restart connections (PageRank's teleport reborn) hold it; jumping knowledge lets nodes choose their depth.
- **Controlled ablation** (@alg-w07-ablation) — one factor, multiple seeds, fixed budget, error bars; claims cite cells, deltas under 2 s.d. are "within noise".
:::

## Where this leaves us

The zoo is now a table. You can read any message-passing architecture into three
slots, hand-compute the four rows that matter, match every repair component to the
failure it treats — with the failure demonstrated on real curves and real grids, not
asserted — and, most importantly, you own the method that adjudicates all such
claims: the controlled ablation, with seeds, error bars, and conclusions that cite
their cells. That method is the week's real deliverable, and the one this course
most confidently promises will still be earning for you in ten years: architectures
age, experimental discipline compounds. That is also why Lab 7's grading weights
the claims paragraph so heavily: writing three sentences that survive their own
table is harder, and more valuable, than getting sixteen cells to run.

Notice what every architecture today accepted without question: the *messages flow
along edges, one hop per layer*. GraphSAGE sampled the edges, GAT weighted them, GIN
counted across them — nobody defied them. Next week is the midterm (Weeks 1–7; a
sample exam is posted with the Week 8 materials, and HW1's solutions unlock after
the deadline). And
in Week 9, the question underneath this whole lecture gets its theorems: *what can
message passing, as a class, never see?* You have already met the answer's
protagonists — WL from Week 2, the triangles-vs-hexagon pair from Week 6, GIN from
today — and the widget's standing challenge (find multisets that fool all three
aggregators) was a first crack in the ceiling. Week 9 maps the whole ceiling, and
then the course starts drilling through it.
